counterexamples_to_USE_EQUALS_TRUE.basis: R8.P1 is framed as a negative test, with expected state FALSE for the present case. The Supreme Court identifies a specific legal error in the construction of the lease, rather than justifying interference because the High Court preferred another possible conclusion. Its application therefore supports the proposed FALSE evaluation of the mere-disagreement premise.

Sarkar J. expressly adopted the premise that the substantive provisions of the 1958 Act governed the pending revision. The majority took the contrary approach and preserved the earlier substantive statutory ground. The proposed use is valid only as a reconstruction of the competing dissenting interpretation, not as an operative majority premise.

The subletting commenced no later than November 1950. Thus the affirmative post-cutoff temporal premise R6.P2 is false on the judicially accepted facts. This negative application of the temporal condition is supported by both the majority's statutory comparison and the dissent's analysis.

Sarkar J. expressly stated that the appellant had not given the prescribed notice relevant to protection under sections 17 and 18 of the 1958 Act. This supports recording R7.P3 as false within the dissent's factual and legal analysis.
